title: The nine ways of prayer
hook: an early book shows Dominic praying with his whole body: bowing, lying prostrate, standing, reading

segments.voice: Yesterday, contemplate and share: the basin fills first, then spills over. Your line was overflow. Did the warm thought reach the person you pictured? Day one thousand two hundred thirty-five.

Dominic left no handbook on how he prayed. What survives is better, in a way: a record of what people saw. Late at night in a church, a man bows low before the altar. Later he is flat on the stone floor, face down. Later still he is on his feet, arms stretched wide, then reaching straight up, as if trying to touch something just out of reach. Then he sits with a book open on his knees and talks to it, nodding, sometimes smiling. The brothers noticed. An early little book gathered it all and named it: the nine ways of prayer of Saint Dominic. Today, prayer that doesn't stay in the head.
screen: `NO HANDBOOK, ONLY WITNESSES.` → `BOWING, LYING FLAT, ARMS WIDE.` → `A BOOK OPEN ON HIS KNEES.`

segments.voice: Walk through the ways the little book describes. He bows, deeply, the way you'd bow to someone you honor. He lies face down on the ground, the posture of someone with nothing left to offer but himself. He kneels and stands and kneels again, over and over, like a person knocking at a door. He stands upright with his hands open in front of him, as if he were reading from a book. He stretches his arms out like a cross. He reaches up high. He sits and reads, quietly, as if in conversation. And on the road, walking from town to town, he prays as he goes. The book ties these postures to scripture, and the Psalms are full of them. In the Douay-Rheims: "Let my prayer be directed as incense in thy sight; the lifting up of my hands, as evening sacrifice." Lifted hands are a prayer the psalmist expects God to notice. Why would a preacher, a man of words, pray so much with his body? The idea underneath the little book, in substance, runs both ways: the soul moves the body, and the body in turn stirs the soul. Kneel and you remember you're small. Open your hands and you remember you're receiving. Catholics still do something like this at Mass: standing for the Gospel, kneeling at the consecration, bowing during the Creed. Dominic just did it alone, at night, with no one watching. Except someone was.
screen: `BOWING, LYING FLAT, KNEELING AGAIN.` · `HANDS OPEN LIKE A BOOK; ARMS LIKE A CROSS.` · `SITTING WITH A BOOK; WALKING THE ROAD.` · `THE BODY STIRS THE SOUL.` · then, large: `THE LIFTING UP OF MY HANDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray in a new posture. Pick one you don't usually use. If you can stand, stand, and hold your hands open in front of you, palms up, like an open book. If kneeling suits you, kneel. If you're sitting, lift your hands a little from your lap. Whatever you choose, stay with it. Notice what it does. Open hands feel different from folded ones. If you pray, let the posture be the prayer, with or without words; you might say the line from the psalm about lifted hands. If you don't, simply breathe in the posture and notice how your body holds the moment. The bell holds the time.
The nine ways of prayer. An early book's record of Dominic praying with his whole body: bowing, lying flat, standing, reaching, reading, walking. Today's word.
screen: `THE NINE WAYS OF PRAYER — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the body prays. Today, once, let your body say something before your words do: a bow of the head, open hands, a pause on your knees by the bed. Day one thousand two hundred thirty-five.

howItsDone: Catholics pray with posture at Mass, standing for the Gospel, kneeling at the consecration and bowing in the Creed; Dominicans still read and teach the early book on the ways Saint Dominic prayed.

fork.setup: you're a young friar. you want to learn to pray like Dominic, but he has written nothing about how he prays. what do you do?
options: ask him for his method in writing.
watch how he prays, and write down what you see.
wait for him to preach a sermon on it.
fork.reveal: that's what survives: an early little book of what people saw, bowing, lying flat, arms wide, reading, walking. prayer learned by watching.

original.note: Latin: a way of praying. the early book describes Dominic's ways of prayer, one posture at a time.

notes: The Nine Ways of Prayer is anonymous, usually dated to the late 13th century and associated with Bologna; the voice says only 'an early little book'. Confirm.

One of the nine ways (the third) involves Dominic disciplining himself with an iron chain; it is left out of the voice and replaced by the kneeling-and-standing way. A Keeper may wish to mention it honestly.
'The soul moves the body, and the body in turn stirs the soul' paraphrases the prologue of the Nine Ways; confirm the paraphrase.
The hook's night-time church scene and the brothers watching are drawn from the book's framing (witnesses such as Sister Cecilia are named in related sources); confirm it is fair.
Douay-Rheims wording of Psalm 140:2 to confirm.
howItsDone: the Mass postures are general Latin-rite practice; confirm.

Editor: 'without thinking about it' cut (said what Catholics think); 'bowing at the name of Jesus in the Creed' corrected to 'bowing during the Creed' (the Creed's bow is at the words on the Incarnation).
